hints: Look closely at what the question asks for, the Ar of copper only, not the whole alloy mixture.
Identify which two peaks belong to copper isotopes, $^{63}\text{Cu}$ at 56.36% and $^{65}\text{Cu}$ at 25.14%, and set aside the gold peak at 197.
Remember Ar is a weighted average, so divide the copper-only total by the copper-only total abundance to rescale to 100% copper.
walkthrough:
**Spot which peaks belong to which element**

Copper has two isotopes in the spectrum, at $m/e$ 63 and 65. Gold has only one peak at $m/e$ 197.

So for copper: $^{63}\text{Cu}$ = 56.36%, $^{65}\text{Cu}$ = 25.14%

**Recall the weighted average rule for Ar**

Ar is the abundance-weighted average of the isotopes of that one element.

$$A_r = \frac{\sum (\text{isotopic mass} \times \text{percentage abundance})}{\sum (\text{percentage abundance of those isotopes})}$$

**Apply it to copper only**

We must ignore gold completely, both on top and bottom. We only weight the two copper isotopes and divide by their combined abundance.

$$A_r(\text{Cu}) = \frac{(56.36 \times 63) + (25.14 \times 65)}{(56.36 + 25.14)}$$

**Check why gold is left out**

Including the 18.50% gold peak would give the average mass of an atom in the alloy, not the Ar of the element copper. That is a classic trap here.

options.A: Numerator is correct for copper, but denominator wrongly adds the 18.50% gold abundance. This dilutes the average and does not rescale to 100% copper, so it gives a value that is too low.
options.B: This includes $(18.50 \times 197)$ on top and 18.50 below. That calculates the average mass of an atom in the copper-gold alloy mixture, not the Ar of the element copper.
options.C: This correctly uses only the two copper isotopes. The top weights each copper mass by its abundance, and the bottom divides by the total copper abundance (56.36 + 25.14) to give the proper weighted average Ar for copper.
options.D: Dividing by $(63 + 65)$ is a confusion error. The bottom of an Ar calculation must be the sum of abundances, not the sum of mass numbers. Mass numbers have no place in the denominator.
